summary: Defines requirements for IPv6 nodes so that IPv6 can function well and interoperate in many devices and situations. It is informational and was later replaced by RFC 6434.

eli5.summary: A checklist for what any device must be able to do to use the newer internet addresses.

questions: what must an ipv6 host support
what must an ipv6 node support
is ipsec mandatory for ipv6 nodes
what is the difference between an ipv6 host and router
subtitle: A one-stop checklist of what every IPv6 host and router must, should or may implement.

tldr.problem: IPv6 spans many specifications, and implementers of hosts, routers and embedded devices had no single list saying which pieces they have to support to interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC walks through the link layer, IP layer, DNS, DHCP, transition, mobility, security and management, and assigns each item a requirement level (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) by pointing to the specification that defines it.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational summary that does not update any Standards Track RFC. It has been obsoleted by RFC 6434 and updated by RFC 5095.

today: RFC 4294 is Informational and has been obsoleted by RFC 6434, which is the current node requirements document. It was also updated by RFC 5095.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 4294 defines the common functionality required from both IPv6 hosts and routers. Many nodes will implement more, but the document gathers requirements from other Standards Track documents in one place. It avoids protocol detail and refers to the relevant RFCs instead. It is informational and does not update Standards Track RFCs.

It uses the definitions from RFC 2460: a node is a device that implements IPv6, a router is a node that forwards IPv6 packets not addressed to itself, and a host is any node that is not a router. Because the exact use of IPv6 in a node is not always known, the overriding requirement is to follow Postel's Robustness Principle: be conservative in what you do and liberal in what you accept.
sections.eli5: The paper does not teach how the language works. It just points to the right books and says which ones every device has to read.

sections.title: Link Layer and IP Layer Requirements
sections.content:
An IPv6 node must support one or more IPv6 link-layer specifications, depending on its hardware. Nodes supporting IPv6 over Ethernet, PPP or ATM MUST implement the matching specification. A minimally conforming IPv6 over ATM driver SHALL support PVC mode.

At the IP layer, RFC 2460 MUST be supported. Nodes MUST always be able to send, receive and process fragment headers. Every conformant implementation MUST be able to send and receive packets, but forwarding is a MAY. A full implementation includes the Hop-by-Hop Options, Routing (Type 0), Fragment, Destination Options, Authentication and Encapsulating Security Payload headers, and a node MUST be able to process them. ICMPv6 MUST be supported.

Neighbor Discovery SHOULD be supported, but within it Router Discovery, Prefix Discovery, Neighbor Unreachability Detection on host paths, Duplicate Address Detection, and sending and receiving Neighbor Solicitation and Advertisement are all MUST. Hosts MUST send Router Solicitations and process Router Advertisements. Redirect SHOULD be supported, and MUST be on routers. Path MTU Discovery SHOULD be supported, though minimal implementations MAY avoid large packets. IPv6 Jumbograms MAY be supported.
sections.eli5: Every device has to know how to build and read the basic IPv6 envelope and how to find its neighbors. Extras like giant envelopes are optional.

sections.title: Addressing and Configuration
sections.content:
The IPv6 Addressing Architecture (RFC 3513, as updated by RFC 3879) MUST be supported. Stateless Address Autoconfiguration (RFC 2462) MUST be supported by hosts, and routers MUST be able to generate link-local addresses. Duplicate Address Detection MUST be supported.

Privacy Extensions for address configuration (RFC 3041) SHOULD be supported. The RFC recommends that this be configurable per connection, because some applications do not work with addresses generated this way. The Default Address Selection rules MUST be implemented, since nodes will often have several addresses.

Stateful autoconfiguration with DHCPv6 (RFC 3315) MAY be supported. The RFC warns that a node without it may be unable to get any address beyond link-local, or other configuration such as DNS server addresses, when a Router Advertisement sets the 'M' or 'O' flags. Nodes that use DHCP for addresses or other information act on those flags. Nodes that do not may ignore them.
sections.eli5: A device has to be able to pick its own address and check that nobody else is using it. Asking a helper server for an address is allowed but not required.

sections.title: DNS, Transition, Mobility and Multicast
sections.content:
Nodes that need to resolve names SHOULD implement a stub resolver with support for AAAA records, reverse lookup under ip6.arpa using PTR records, and EDNS0 to allow DNS packets larger than 512 octets. DNS security extensions are RECOMMENDED, and the experimental A6 and DNAME records are NOT RECOMMENDED.

IPv6 nodes MAY support IPv4. If a node implements dual stack and tunneling, then RFC 4213 MUST be supported.

For multicast, nodes that need to join groups SHOULD implement MLDv2. A node whose applications need only Any-Source Multicast MAY implement MLDv1 instead, and a node that needs Source-Specific Multicast MUST support MLDv2.

For Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775), hosts MAY support mobile node functionality and SHOULD support route optimization for correspondent nodes. Routers SHOULD support the generic mobility requirements for all IPv6 routers and MAY act as home agents. Network management is a MAY, though for embedded devices it may be the only way to control them. Nodes with an SNMP agent SHOULD support the IP Forwarding Table MIB and the IP MIB.
sections.eli5: If a device needs to look up names, it should understand the new address records. Talking old IPv4 as well, moving between networks, and remote management are all extras to add when they make sense.

sections.title: IPsec Requirements and Security
sections.content:
The IPsec Security Architecture (RFC 4301) MUST be supported, and so must both ESP (RFC 4303) and AH (RFC 4302). Nodes SHOULD follow the algorithm requirements in RFC 4305. Support for the NULL encryption and NULL authentication algorithms MUST be provided, but they MUST NOT both be NULL.

DES-CBC SHOULD NOT be supported within ESP, because DES provides 56 bits of protection, which is no longer considered sufficient. HMAC-SHA-1-96 MUST be supported, HMAC-MD5-96 MAY be, and 3DES-CBC and AES-128-CBC MUST be supported in ESP.

Manual configuration of the key and SPI MUST be supported. Automated key management SHOULD be supported, and MUST be where key refresh, anti-replay or on-demand Security Association creation is needed.

The Security Considerations section says the document does not affect the security of the Internet, but that implementations are expected to support a minimum set of security features.
sections.eli5: Every device must know how to lock its messages with the standard IPsec locks. The old weak lock called DES is not recommended any more.
